prompt.context_jp: S&F商事の会議室では、水産部と営業部___本マグロを巡って睨み合っていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 水産部と営業部___本マグロを巡って睨み合っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that introduces the two departments as new, specific actors in the scene.

feedback.correct_en: This sentence opens the chapter — the two departments are being newly introduced as the subjects doing the glaring. が marks that newly-presented information.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat the departments as an already-established topic, but they haven't been introduced yet in this chapter.

contrast_examples.jp: 部屋には二つの派閥がある。その派閥は仲が悪い。
contrast_examples.en: There are two factions in the room. Those factions get along poorly. (first が introduces, then は takes it up as topic)

prompt.context_jp: The heated argument is suddenly interrupted by...
prompt.prompt_jp: 熱いお茶の湯気___、白熱した議論の隙間に滑り込んだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for this suddenly-appearing new element.

feedback.correct_en: The steam is a brand-new element intruding into the scene — が spotlights it as fresh, perceived information at this dramatic moment.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame the steam as a known topic, draining it of its startling 'something new slipped in' effect.

contrast_examples.jp: 静けさの中、鈴の音が聞こえた。
contrast_examples.en: In the stillness, (suddenly) a bell sounded.

contrast_examples.jp: その鈴は祖母のものだ。
contrast_examples.en: That bell belongs to my grandmother.

prompt.context_jp: 美雪 is being introduced into the scene for the first time.
prompt.prompt_jp: 派遣の森美雪の手___緊張で固まり、湯呑みがわずかに傾いだ…
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that presents Miyuki's hand as newly-perceived subject.

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is zooming in on a new, momentary event — Miyuki's hand stiffening. が picks it out as freshly-noticed information.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would set her hand up as an ongoing topic, which clashes with the sudden-event feel of this description.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の手が震えた。
contrast_examples.en: Her hand trembled. (observed event)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の手はいつも冷たい。
contrast_examples.en: Her hands are always cold. (characteristic topic)

prompt.context_jp: After spilling the tea...
prompt.prompt_jp: 美雪___言葉にならないまま頭を下げ続け、頬は真っ赤に染まっていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that marks Miyuki as the ongoing topic of this descriptive sentence.

feedback.correct_en: Miyuki has already been introduced; now the narrator describes two things about her (bowing, blushing cheeks). は establishes her as the topic for that extended description.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would spotlight her as new/exclusive information, but she is already in focus and the sentence is painting her ongoing state.

contrast_examples.jp: 美雪は黙っていた。
contrast_examples.en: Miyuki (as for her) stayed silent.

contrast_examples.jp: 美雪が黙った。
contrast_examples.en: It was Miyuki who went silent.

prompt.context_jp: Describing Haruko calmly handling the spill, in contrast to Miyuki's panic.
prompt.prompt_jp: 動作に一切の狼狽___ない。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that gives emphatic, contrastive 'not even a trace' feel.

feedback.correct_en: 〜はない with an emphatic noun ('a trace of panic') carries a contrastive 'as for panic — none at all' nuance, implicitly contrasting Haruko with the flustered Miyuki.
feedback.incorrect_en: 〜がない would just state the plain absence; it loses the pointed, emphatic contrast the narrator is drawing.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼には迷いはない。
contrast_examples.en: He has no hesitation (whatsoever).

contrast_examples.jp: そこには椅子がない。
contrast_examples.en: There's no chair there. (plain fact)

prompt.context_jp: The vice president reflecting on the departmental standoff.
prompt.prompt_jp: マグロ___水産と営業のどちらに任せても揉める…
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that sets up 'tuna' as the topic being commented on.

feedback.correct_en: The tuna project is already the known subject of the meeting; the sentence makes a general comment about it ('as for the tuna, no matter who gets it...'). は fits that topic-and-comment structure.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would newly single out tuna as the one thing that causes trouble — but here tuna is background context, not fresh information.

contrast_examples.jp: この案件は誰がやっても難しい。
contrast_examples.en: This project is hard no matter who does it.

contrast_examples.jp: この案件が一番難しい。
contrast_examples.en: This project is the hardest one. (exhaustive listing)

prompt.context_jp: The coworkers are gossiping over the embarrassing emails. Meanwhile...
prompt.prompt_jp: 当の春子___、隣の席で無表情のままモニターを見つめている。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that signals contrast with the gossiping coworkers.

feedback.correct_en: The narration pivots from the gossiping group to Haruko herself — 当の春子は carries contrastive 'as for Haruko, the one actually named'. は delivers that pivot.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present her as newly-noticed, but she's already the center of the gossip; the sentence contrasts her behavior with the others'.

contrast_examples.jp: みんなは騒いだ。彼女は静かだった。
contrast_examples.en: Everyone made a fuss. She, by contrast, was quiet.

prompt.context_jp: The emails name Haruko, but the red sweater belonged to Miyuki.
prompt.prompt_jp: 名指しされているのは春子だが、赤いセーターを着ていたの___会議室で震えていた美雪の方だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle completing the contrastive 'A on one side, B on the other' structure.

feedback.correct_en: This is a classic 〜のはAだが、〜のはBだ contrastive frame. は on both halves lines them up explicitly against each other (named = Haruko / sweater-wearer = Miyuki).
feedback.incorrect_en: が would break the parallel contrast and make the second clause sound like isolated new info rather than the matching counterweight.

contrast_examples.jp: 話したのは私だが、聞いていたのは彼だ。
contrast_examples.en: The one who spoke was me, but the one listening was him.

prompt.context_jp: The narration has described how everyone saw temps as outsiders. Then...
prompt.prompt_jp: だが、その線引きを笑うように現れた女___一人いた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for this dramatic 'there was one woman...' introduction.

feedback.correct_en: This is a storybook 'there existed one such person' introduction — classic existential が, presenting a brand-new character onto the stage.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would need the woman to already be known; here she's being revealed to us for the first time with narrative flourish.

contrast_examples.jp: 昔々、おじいさんがいました。
contrast_examples.en: Long ago, there was an old man. (existential が)

contrast_examples.jp: そのおじいさんは山へ行きました。
contrast_examples.en: That old man went into the mountain. (now topicalized)

prompt.context_jp: The three sit down for lunch and chat.
prompt.prompt_jp: 話題___自然と、いつも一人で外食する春子のことへ流れていった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that marks 'the conversation topic' as the sentence's topic.

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is commenting on what the ongoing conversation did — 話題は flows as topic ('as for the talk, it drifted toward...'). は fits general commentary on an established frame.
feedback.incorrect_en: 話題が would spotlight 'conversation' as new/exclusive, but conversations are the natural ongoing frame here, not fresh information.

contrast_examples.jp: 話は昔の恋人の方へ流れた。
contrast_examples.en: The talk drifted toward old flames. (topic commentary)

prompt.context_jp: Haruko has just dropped market numbers that undercut the sales team.
prompt.prompt_jp: 部屋の空気___一気に片側に傾き、里中は思わず息を呑んだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for this sudden perceived change.

feedback.correct_en: A sudden shift being observed and reported in the moment — が marks 'the atmosphere' as newly-perceived subject of a sudden event.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make it sound like a general property of the room ('as for the atmosphere, it leans...'), losing the suddenness.

contrast_examples.jp: 空気が変わった。
contrast_examples.en: The air changed. (something just happened)

contrast_examples.jp: この部屋は空気が重い。
contrast_examples.en: This room has heavy air. (general trait)

prompt.context_jp: Miyuki squints at the back of the restaurant and —
prompt.prompt_jp: …美雪の視界に、テレビでしか見たことのない解体師ツネの姿___飛び込んできた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for Tsune's figure suddenly entering her field of vision.

feedback.correct_en: 〜が飛び込んできた is a canonical 'something new/startling appeared' pattern. が highlights Tsune's figure as freshly-perceived.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat Tsune as a known topic, but the whole point is Miyuki spotting him by surprise.

contrast_examples.jp: 子猫が飛び込んできた。
contrast_examples.en: A kitten rushed in. (new, unexpected)

prompt.context_jp: Miyuki approaches Haruko's seat at the diner.
prompt.prompt_jp: 近づく足音を、春子___箸を止めずに聞いていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle marking Haruko as the ongoing topic/doer being described.

feedback.correct_en: Haruko is the established figure of this scene; the sentence comments on her behavior ('as for Haruko, she kept eating...'). は fits that topic-comment flow.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would newly identify Haruko as the hearer, but the whole paragraph is already centered on her — no new identification needed.

contrast_examples.jp: その音を彼女は無視した。
contrast_examples.en: That sound — she ignored it. (she as topic)

prompt.context_jp: After Haruko's data silences everyone...
prompt.prompt_jp: 反論のできない沈黙___、蛍光灯の音だけを浮かび上がらせた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for this newly-arising silence.

feedback.correct_en: The silence is a newly-arisen state being pointed out as the cause of the fluorescent-light sound surfacing. が introduces it as fresh, specific subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat the silence as an established topic, but it's just now descended on the room — fresh, dramatic information.

contrast_examples.jp: 重い沈黙が部屋を満たした。
contrast_examples.en: A heavy silence filled the room. (new event)

prompt.context_jp: After the fall at the loading dock...
prompt.prompt_jp: 冷え切った搬入口の中央に、ツネ___右腕を庇うようにして倒れていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle presenting the discovered scene.

feedback.correct_en: This is a 'there/in that place, X was V-ing' discovery scene. が marks Tsune as the newly-perceived subject the reader's eye is drawn to.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would read as general commentary on Tsune, but the sentence is a dramatic snapshot of what the characters find in the loading bay.

contrast_examples.jp: ドアの前に男が倒れていた。
contrast_examples.en: A man lay collapsed in front of the door. (discovery scene)

prompt.context_jp: Right after the tea spills.
prompt.prompt_jp: 水産部の一人___思わず膝を引き、椅子の軋みが会議室を裂いた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle introducing this reflexive movement.

feedback.correct_en: An unspecified 'one of them' is picked out mid-scene as the one who flinched. が fits the newly-introduced, non-topical subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: は needs a known/established referent; '一人' here is an indefinite 'one of them' being newly singled out.

contrast_examples.jp: 観客の一人が立ち上がった。
contrast_examples.en: One of the audience stood up. (indefinite, new)

prompt.context_jp: When asked about managing Haruko, Ichitsuki's complaints pour out...
prompt.prompt_jp: 話を振られると、その苦労話は___のように次々と溢れ出す。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the idiom meaning 'in one's element / unstoppable once started'.

feedback.correct_en: 水を得た魚のように ('like a fish that got water') is the set simile for someone suddenly in their element and gushing freely — exactly how Ichitsuki unloads his complaints.
feedback.incorrect_en: 鯉の滝登り is about dramatic success/rise. 井の中の蛙 means 'narrow-minded person' — neither fits an outpouring of talk.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は料理の話になると水を得た魚だ。
contrast_examples.en: When talk turns to cooking, he's in his element.

prompt.context_jp: On solo karaoke, solo yakiniku...
prompt.prompt_jp: そういうのが___きだしたら 女は おしまいだよ
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the idiom meaning 'when it starts to suit you / become natural to you'.

feedback.correct_en: 板につく means a role or behavior has become natural/fitting for someone — Ichitsuki's complaint is that once solo activities start to 'look right' on a woman, she's lost her way (in his view).
feedback.incorrect_en: 腰を据える = settle in to tackle something. 気を抜く = let one's guard down. Neither captures 'becoming second nature'.

contrast_examples.jp: 司会が板についてきたね。
contrast_examples.en: You've really grown into the MC role.

prompt.context_jp: Ichitsuki dismisses the idea that Haruko gets lonely.
prompt.prompt_jp: “寂しい”なんちゅうのはね 人間の持つデリケートな感情だよ ___なんか 感情なんかないから
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the term Ichitsuki uses to belittle Haruko as emotionless loner.

feedback.correct_en: 一匹狼 ('lone wolf') is the recurring label the men pin on Haruko throughout this chapter — a person who acts alone without needing group ties.
feedback.incorrect_en: 八方美人 means 'everybody's friend/people-pleaser' — opposite nuance. 猫かぶり means 'hiding true nature' — different idea.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は社内でも一匹狼だ。
contrast_examples.en: He's a lone wolf even inside the company.

prompt.context_jp: Miyuki wants Haruko to correct the misdirected emails. Haruko shrugs:
prompt.prompt_jp: 誤解を___のも面倒くさいのよ
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb that collocates with 誤解.

feedback.correct_en: 誤解を解く ('clear up a misunderstanding') is the fixed collocation — the misunderstanding is 'untangled', not opened or repaired.
feedback.incorrect_en: 開く literally means 'open'; 直す means 'fix/repair' (used with 間違い but not 誤解). Neither forms a natural phrase with 誤解.

contrast_examples.jp: どうか誤解を解いてください。
contrast_examples.en: Please clear up the misunderstanding.

prompt.context_jp: The sales rep dismissing the fisheries dept's proposal, politely-but-sarcastically.
prompt.prompt_jp: 「___ ご意見だとは思いますが 水産部は 買い付けだけ やってもらえますか？」
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the adjective that lets you accept-then-reject in a business-polite way.

feedback.correct_en: 結構な~だとは思いますが is a stock 'that's a fine idea, however...' preface — polite surface, dismissive underneath. Perfect for office pushback.
feedback.incorrect_en: すごい is too casual for business. 普通の ('ordinary') would already insult the proposal rather than feigning respect.

contrast_examples.jp: 結構なご提案ですが、再検討をお願いします。
contrast_examples.en: A fine suggestion, but please reconsider.

prompt.context_jp: Asked for 'winning tips' for group dates, Haruko snaps:
prompt.prompt_jp: 「___者の知恵比べに 勝者なし」
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the word that gives this cutting put-down its edge.

feedback.correct_en: 愚か者 ('fools') makes the proverb-like line bite: 'a wisdom-contest among fools has no winner'. It matches Haruko's cold dismissal of the gōkon crowd.
feedback.incorrect_en: 勇敢 ('brave') and 正直 ('honest') are positive — they'd flip the insult into praise, which doesn't fit the scene at all.

contrast_examples.jp: 愚か者同士の争いだ。
contrast_examples.en: A squabble among fools.

prompt.context_jp: Haruko's dismissal of Miyuki's new 'lunch friends':
prompt.prompt_jp: そんなの友達じゃなくて ___のフンだね
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the noun completing Haruko's biting metaphor for hangers-on.

feedback.correct_en: 金魚のフン ('goldfish droppings') is a fixed idiom for people who trail along behind others uselessly — exactly Haruko's dig at Miyuki's new group.
feedback.incorrect_en: 犬のフン and 鳥のフン are literal animal droppings but carry no 'hanger-on' idiomatic meaning in Japanese.

contrast_examples.jp: あの子はいつも金魚のフンみたいについて回る。
contrast_examples.en: That kid always tags along like goldfish droppings.

prompt.context_jp: The narrator describing Haruko's work philosophy.
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼女の___に “不可能”と “残業”の文字は ない
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the noun that makes this a Napoleon-style boast.

feedback.correct_en: 〜の辞書に…の文字はない ('no such word exists in X's dictionary') is a famous idiomatic flourish, originally attributed to Napoleon. It fits the narrator's grand intro of Haruko.
feedback.incorrect_en: 予定 or 鞄 would be literal ('schedule', 'bag') — they break the famous idiom and lose the heroic register.

contrast_examples.jp: 私の辞書に『諦める』の文字はない。
contrast_examples.en: The word 'give up' does not exist in my dictionary.

prompt.context_jp: Shoji sneers 'you can go home now'. Haruko fires back:
prompt.prompt_jp: 「言われなくても帰ります ___します」
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the set phrase for leaving the workplace.

feedback.correct_en: 失礼します is the standard phrase for leaving work/an office — Haruko uses it to coolly cut the exchange short.
feedback.incorrect_en: 拝見します means 'I will look at (humbly)'. ご苦労 is said *to* subordinates, never when leaving.

contrast_examples.jp: お先に失礼します。
contrast_examples.en: I'll be leaving before you (standard office exit).

prompt.context_jp: Opening line of the chapter — introducing the conference-room scene.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds more natural as a scene-setting opening sentence?

choices.text: S&F商事の会議室では、水産部と営業部が本マグロを巡って睨み合っていた。
S&F商事の会議室では、水産部と営業部は本マグロを巡って睨み合っていた。

feedback.correct_en: The opening line introduces both departments fresh. が presents them as new actors in a vivid scene; this is standard for narrative openers.
feedback.incorrect_en: は presupposes the two departments as a known topic — awkward in an opening sentence where readers meet them for the first time.

contrast_examples.jp: ある日、男たちが争っていた。
contrast_examples.en: One day, men were fighting. (opener)

prompt.context_jp: Satonaka gently pointing out that Ogasawara's 'proposal' was really just a personal story.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural as a polite in-meeting correction?

choices.text: それは 案ではなくて 感想ですよね
それは 案じゃない 感想だよ

feedback.correct_en: 〜ではなくて…ですよね softens a correction into a shared observation — appropriate for addressing a senior colleague in a meeting.
feedback.incorrect_en: じゃない…だよ is casual, almost blunt — it would sound rude addressing a senior in a formal meeting setting.

contrast_examples.jp: これは意見ではなくて質問ですよね。
contrast_examples.en: That's not an opinion but a question, isn't it?

prompt.context_jp: Contrasting who is named in the emails vs. who actually wore the red sweater.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version delivers the A-vs-B contrast most naturally?

choices.text: 名指しされているのは春子だが、赤いセーターを着ていたのは美雪の方だった。
春子が名指しされていたが、美雪が赤いセーターを着ていた。

feedback.correct_en: The cleft 〜のは…だ structure explicitly pairs the two contrasts (named one / sweater-wearer), highlighting the mix-up at the heart of the scene.
feedback.incorrect_en: The flat 〜が…が version loses the parallelism and reads as two unrelated facts rather than a pointed juxtaposition.

contrast_examples.jp: 電話したのは兄だが、来たのは弟だった。
contrast_examples.en: The one who called was my older brother, but the one who came was my younger brother.

prompt.context_jp: Shoji dismissing Haruko at end-of-contract time, deliberately rude.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line captures Shoji's blunt, dismissive tone most naturally?

choices.text: あんたの仕事は ここまでだ もう帰っていいよ
大前さんのお仕事はここまででございます お帰りいただいて結構です

feedback.correct_en: あんた and 〜ていいよ carry a put-down tone fitting Shoji's resentment of temp workers. The chapter uses this blunt register deliberately.
feedback.incorrect_en: The hyper-polite version would be comically out of character — Shoji is picking a fight, not showing respect.

contrast_examples.jp: もう帰っていいよ。
contrast_examples.en: You can go home now. (dismissive)

contrast_examples.jp: お先にお帰りください。
contrast_examples.en: Please leave ahead of us. (polite)

prompt.context_jp: Describing Tsune suddenly appearing in Miyuki's field of vision.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing is the natural idiom for 'suddenly caught sight of'?

choices.text: 視界に、ツネの姿が飛び込んできた
視界に、ツネの姿が落ちてきた
視界に、ツネの姿が入ってしまった

feedback.correct_en: 視界に〜が飛び込んでくる is the fixed idiom for something leaping suddenly into one's view — vivid and surprising.
feedback.incorrect_en: 落ちてくる (fall in) and 入ってしまう (end up entering) don't collocate with 視界 for this 'startling glimpse' meaning.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の笑顔が目に飛び込んできた。
contrast_examples.en: His smile leapt into my eyes (I suddenly caught sight of it).
